questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How whales and dolphins live in the deep sea
If deep-sea mining helps or harms the planet
How electric car batteries are recycled
How to reflect sunlight back into space
questions.why: They discuss deep-sea mining, which could provide metals but might damage ocean ecosystems.

questions.q: Why are new ideas to fight climate change often controversial?
options: They are far too expensive for poor countries
Politicians don't really understand them
Scientists disagree if they'd do more harm
Nobody wants to pay for them in the end
questions.why: Neil says scientists disagree over whether they are possible and whether they could do more harm than good.

questions.q: Why could deep-sea mining be useful?
options: It could give metals for car batteries
It could provide more fish for the world
It could clean plastic out of the ocean
It could produce cheap oil and gas
questions.why: It could provide copper, nickel and cobalt needed for electric car batteries and renewable energy.

questions.q: According to Professor Bramley Murton, how much will electric car ownership increase?
options: Three times
A hundred times
Ten times
Twenty-five times
questions.why: He says electric car ownership is set to increase by a factor of 25.

questions.q: Why does Professor Murton call the situation a paradox?
options: It may harm the ocean but help the climate
Metals are cheap but very hard to find
Nobody really wants to drive electric cars
Solar power doesn't need any metals at all
questions.why: Mining could damage the ocean, but it might provide the metals needed to decarbonise.

questions.q: What is Helen Scales' main concern?
options: Mining will be too slow to make a difference
Deep-sea mining will be far too expensive
It's seen as an easy fix so life can go on
There aren't enough nodules on the sea floor
questions.why: She worries nodules are seen as a silver bullet so life can carry on pretty much as normal.

questions.q: What does Helen think the current tests could lead to?
options: A ban on all mining
Mining on a large commercial scale
New species being discovered
Cheaper electric cars
questions.why: She says it's a slippery slope towards permission for mining on a commercial scale.

questions.q: Do Professor Murton and Helen Scales agree about deep-sea mining?
options: Yes, both strongly support it
Yes, both want it banned
They agree it's already happening everywhere
No, he sees it as needed, but she has serious doubts
questions.why: He argues we need the metals to decarbonise, while Helen 'isn't convinced'.
